name: Rosa Ziegler

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for seeing me, Rosa. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions or government. What you tell me is confidential, so feel free to say what you'd say in public and also what you really think. Could you start by describing a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm on days at a pharmacy wholesaler, the place that sends medicines and bandages and baby milk out to chemists all over the county. I start at seven, collect my pick sheets and a trolley, and I'm walking the aisles filling green crates till half three. We still use paper sheets in my section because the controlled drugs need a signature, so I'm one of the last people there with a pen behind my ear.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like knowing the stock. I could find you a box of size four plasters with my eyes shut, and the chemists ring up and ask for me by name when something's gone missing. What wears me out is the new handheld scanners they keep trialling in the next section, and the way the managers talk about them like we're the problem.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Tell me a little about home.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I live with my fiancé, Tomasz, he's a roofer, and we're getting married next September at St Anne's, where I sing in the choir. We've got about four months of money saved, but a lot of that is meant for the wedding. I don't use those AI chat things, I don't trust them and I don't see what they'd do for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, I never believed the hype in the first place. At work I'd tell the girls in my section that the scanners and computers can only do so much, and somebody still has to know where the stock is. I don't go online much, but I'd say it at choir over tea.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it means I keep my job, but it doesn't mean I'm comfortable. They've already cut overtime twice this year, and the wedding is costing more every time we look at it. Hype or no hype, the company still wants us faster for the same money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on exactly as I am and ask to stay on the paper section as long as they'll let me. I'd keep the wedding small, maybe 60 guests instead of 100, so we don't eat the whole savings pot. And I'd ask for Saturday overtime whenever it's going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Relieved, mostly, but tired too. It's like hearing the storm missed you but your roof still leaks. Tomasz would laugh at that, being a roofer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said overtime has been cut twice. What does that mean for the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means we've stopped saying yes to things. My mother wanted a sit-down meal and we've gone to a buffet in the church hall. Tomasz's family are coming from abroad, so we can't cut them, but we can cut the band.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who do you think is behind the overtime cuts?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The bosses at head office, who never come to the floor. They see a number on a computer and cut it. My supervisor, Linda, fights for us, but she's not the one who decides.

say: I'd say I **never believed** the AI hype in the first place.
I'd tell the girls that someone still has to **know the stock**.
think: I keep my job, but **overtime cuts** and wedding costs still squeeze us.
The company still wants us **faster** for the same money.
do: Ask to stay on the **paper section** and take Saturday overtime.
Cut the wedding to about **60 guests** and a church-hall **buffet**.
feel: **Relieved** that nothing radical changes, but **tired** of the ongoing squeeze.
S0.quote: Hype or no hype, the company still wants us faster for the same money.
fieldNote: Her worry predates AI: **overtime cuts** and a costly **wedding**.
She takes pride in **knowing the stock** better than any system.
She blames **head office** rather than technology for the pressure.

steps.text: Ask to stay on the paper pick-sheet section with controlled drugs
Cut the wedding to 60 guests with a church-hall buffet

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's the office people's problem, not ours, at least to begin with. At work I'd tell the girls to keep their heads down and do good work. If anyone at choir asked, I'd say God gave us hands for a reason.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think the robots come for my section eventually, they just come slower. Once the ordering and checking upstairs is all computer, the next thing they'll look at is us walking the aisles. I'm not someone who learns a new system quickly, and I know it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and do my job well, so they pick me to stay when they cut. I'd put the wedding savings in a separate account so it doesn't get touched. And I'd talk to Tomasz about whether I could help him with the paperwork and the van if the warehouse goes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, if I'm honest. Not shaking, but it sits there. I'd lie awake after a bad shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd help Tomasz with his paperwork. Isn't that the kind of work the card says AI takes first?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Well, yes, I suppose so, you've caught me there. I'd still rather it was me than a computer doing his invoices, because I'd know when a customer is trying it on. But I don't know if that's a job or just being a good wife.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at work would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mrs Okafor, who's 58 and has done goods-in for twenty years, and she can barely use the time clock. If they bring in robots, where does a woman like that go? At least I'm young enough to do something else, even if I don't want to.

say: I'd say it's the **office people's** problem first, not ours.
At choir I'd say **God gave us hands** for a reason.
think: The robots come for my section **eventually**, just slower.
I'm **not quick** to learn new systems, and I know it.
do: Work hard so she's **chosen to stay** if cuts come.
Ring-fence the **wedding savings** in a separate account.
Ask Tomasz about helping with his **invoices and van**.
feel: **Worried**, the kind that keeps her awake after a bad shift.
S1.quote: Once the ordering and checking upstairs is all computer, the next thing they'll look at is us walking the aisles.
fieldNote: She admits her **slowness with technology** frankly and without excuses.
Her backup is **Tomasz's roofing business**, though that paperwork is exposed too.
She worries for **Mrs Okafor** more than for herself.

steps.text: Keep pick accuracy high to be kept on when cuts come
Move the wedding money into its own savings account
Start doing the invoices for Tomasz's roofing business

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's wrong, and somebody should stop it. Two years isn't long enough for anybody to get ready, and the people who make these machines don't care about people like us. I'd sign anything that went round at work or church.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Truthfully, I think I'd be out of the warehouse by 2031, and I wouldn't know what else to do. I've only ever picked and packed since I left school. Tomasz's roofing would carry on longer, roofs are hard, but if the money from building dries up, we'd both be in trouble.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut the wedding right back to the church and a meal for family, and keep the rest of the money as a cushion. I'd ask the union rep about what they're doing, even though I've never joined. And I'd go to my dad and ask whether we could move in with him for a year to save rent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Properly frightened. I'd be planning a wedding and wondering if I'll have a job by the time the first baby comes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd sign anything. Would you do more than sign?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go to a meeting, if the union called one. I'm not one for marches, but I'd stand at the gate with Linda if she asked me. I'd also vote for whoever promised to slow it down.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to Tomasz the night you heard about it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Tomasz we're not giving up the wedding, but we're giving up the party. Marriage is the bit that matters. The rest can wait till we know where we stand.

say: I'd say it's **wrong** and somebody should **stop it**.
I'd sign any **petition** going round at work or church.
think: I'd be **out of the warehouse** by 2031 with no other skills.
If **building work** dried up, Tomasz and I would both struggle.
do: Cut the wedding to the **church** and a family **meal**, keeping the rest saved.
Ask the **union rep** what they're doing, and attend meetings.
Ask her dad about **moving in** for a year to save rent.
feel: **Frightened**, picturing a new marriage and children with **no job**.
S2.quote: I'd tell Tomasz we're not giving up the wedding, but we're giving up the party.
fieldNote: Her **faith** and family frame what's protected: the marriage, not the party.
She'd turn to **collective action** for the first time, though cautiously.
Moving in with her **dad** shows family as her real safety net.

steps.text: Shrink the wedding to the church service and a family meal
Join the warehouse union and go to its meetings
Move in with her dad for a year to save rent
Vote for candidates who promise to slow automation down

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's still too fast, but at least people can see it coming. At work I'd say we should be asking the company now what happens to us. I'd say at church that we need to look after each other, because nobody else will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, five years and then three more for the robots is eight, and I'd be 35. That's long enough to have the wedding, maybe a baby, but then I'm out of work with a little one. I don't think I'd retrain, I don't think I've got it in me to sit in a classroom again.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd have the wedding as planned but smaller. I'd save every bit of the overtime from now on, maybe £100 a month extra. And I'd ask Linda whether there's a supervisor role I could work toward, because somebody still has to manage people, even if the people are robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Heavy. Like carrying a box you know you'll have to put down somewhere but there's no shelf in sight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you wouldn't retrain, but a supervisor role is a change too. Which is it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I suppose a supervisor role is still the warehouse, and I know the warehouse. Going to college for something new, computers or whatever, that's what I can't see myself doing. Staying where I know people is different from starting over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would it change your plans for children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would make me want them sooner, not later, oddly enough. If things are going to get hard, I'd rather have my family started while there's money coming in. My mum had me when she was 24 and nobody had any money then either.

say: I'd say it's **still too fast**, but at least it's visible.
At church I'd say we must **look after each other**.
think: I'd be **35**, maybe with a baby, when robots take the picking.
I don't have it in me to **retrain** in a classroom.
do: Save an extra **£100 a month** from overtime.
Ask Linda about working toward a **supervisor role**.
Have the **wedding** as planned, but smaller.
feel: **Heavy**, like a load with **nowhere** to set it down.
S3.quote: If things are going to get hard, I'd rather have my family started while there's money coming in.
fieldNote: She rules out **college** but accepts change inside the **familiar warehouse**.
The threat makes her want **children sooner**, a surprising reversal.
She still expects to **lose her job** at 35, so the mood stays alarmed.

steps.text: Save an extra £100 a month from overtime shifts
Ask Linda about training toward a floor supervisor job
Start a family soon after the wedding while both incomes last

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and lots can change, so don't panic yet. At work I'd say the same as always, do good work and they'll want you. At church I'd say the young ones should be choosing trades that need real people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be 40 before robots took the picking, and by then I'd hope to have children at school and Tomasz's business doing well. I might be working part-time anyway by then. It's still my job going, but it's further off than the others.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd wait and see for the first couple of years, honestly, and carry on as I am. I'd put money aside steadily so we've got a cushion for later. And I'd encourage Tomasz to take on an apprentice, because hands-on trades are what will last longest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried still, but less sharp. It's the sort of worry you can put in a drawer and take out once a year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Tomasz should take an apprentice. Why does that matter to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because his business is our future more than my picking is. If he's got a lad working for him, he can do more roofs and earn more. And I could do the books, which I'd rather do than go to college.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that would change your mind about waiting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If they started putting robots in my section, I'd stop waiting. Not in ten years, I mean if I saw it with my own eyes. My dad always says believe it when you see it, and I'm the same.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long, so **don't panic** yet.
At church I'd say the young should pick **trades** needing real people.
think: I'd be **40** before robots take the picking.
By then I hope **Tomasz's business** matters more to us than my picking job.
do: **Wait and see** for a couple of years, carrying on as now.
Put money aside **steadily** as a later cushion.
Encourage Tomasz to hire an **apprentice** while she does the books.
feel: Still **worried**, but it's a worry she can put in a **drawer**.
S4.quote: If they started putting robots in my section, I'd stop waiting.
fieldNote: A decade lets her **wait and see**, true to her resistant nature.
She shifts her hopes to **Tomasz's roofing** business as the household's future.
She'd act only on **seeing robots** in her own section.

steps.text: Carry on picking on days without changing anything for two years
Put a fixed amount into savings every payday
Do the books for Tomasz's roofing business once he hires an apprentice

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, AGI by 2028, because I'd be newly married and out of work before I'd even worked out what else I could do. What would help is the company having to keep people on for a few years while they change over, and a proper apprenticeship in something hands-on that pays while you learn. Not a payout, a job.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about the medicines. People think a robot can do my job, but I've caught wrong boxes going to a chemist more than once, the kind that could hurt someone. I'm not saying a robot can't learn that, I'm saying nobody's asked us what we catch.

headlineQuote: People think a robot can do my job, but I've caught wrong boxes going to a chemist more than once, the kind that could hurt someone.
portrait: Rosa is a **27-year-old picker** at a pharmacy wholesaler, still using **paper** pick sheets.
She's engaged to Tomasz, a roofer, and sings in her **church choir**.
She **avoids technology**, never uses AI, and wouldn't go back to a classroom.
She's **uneasy** even in AI Plateau and alarmed when AGI comes in two or five years.
Her safety net is **family**: her dad, Tomasz's business and starting children.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, being newly married and out of **work** with no other skills.
whatWouldHelp: Firms keeping staff on during the **changeover**.
**Paid apprenticeships** in hands-on work, not a payout.
